Abstract Algebra — 05 · Field Extensions and Galois Theory

Created2026-01-14|Updated2026-01-14|Mathematics > Abstract Algebra
|Post View:

Post 04 ended by building new fields: C=R[x]/(x2+1)\mathbb{C} = \mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2+1)C=R[x]/(x2+1) and F4=F2[x]/(x2+x+1)\mathbb{F}_4 = \mathbb{F}_2[x]/(x^2+x+1)F4​=F2​[x]/(x2+x+1). This post studies such constructions systematically. A bigger field EEE containing FFF is a vector space over FFF, and its dimension, the degree, turns out to be a very strong invariant: a single divisibility argument proves that no ruler-and-compass construction doubles a cube or trisects a 60° angle. Galois theory then attaches to a polynomial a finite group, the permutations of its roots that respect all algebraic relations, and the Fundamental Theorem matches the subfields of the splitting field with the subgroups of that group. Everything from posts 01–04 comes together here: groups, normal subgroups and quotients, group actions, Sylow-type counting, irreducible polynomials and quotient rings. The chapter ends with the reason there is no quintic formula.

Series map: 00 Integers, Relations & Modular Arithmetic → 01 Groups & Subgroups → 02 Cosets, Lagrange & Quotient Groups → 03 Homomorphisms, Group Actions & Sylow → 04 Rings, Ideals & Fields → 05 Field Extensions & Galois Theory (this post).

Learning Outcome

  • Compute the degree of a field extension, and prove and use the tower law.
  • Find minimal polynomials, and prove that F(α)≅F[x]/(mα)F(\alpha) \cong F[x]/(m_\alpha)F(α)≅F[x]/(mα​) with degree deg⁡mα\deg m_\alphadegmα​.
  • Show that Q(2,3)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2, \sqrt3)Q(2​,3​) has degree 4 and is generated by 2+3\sqrt2 + \sqrt32​+3​.
  • Prove that doubling the cube and trisecting a 60° angle are impossible with ruler and compass.
  • Build splitting fields, and prove that there is one finite field of each prime-power order, up to isomorphism.
  • Define separable, normal and Galois extensions and the Galois group.
  • State the Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory and draw the subfield/subgroup lattices for Q(2,3)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2, \sqrt3)Q(2​,3​) and for the splitting field of x3−2x^3 - 2x3−2.
  • Define solvable groups and outline why the roots of x5−4x+2x^5 - 4x + 2x5−4x+2 cannot be written with radicals.

Chapter 1 — Field extensions and degree

Terminology

  • Extension — a pair of fields F⊆EF \subseteq EF⊆E, written E/FE/FE/F ("EEE over FFF"). FFF is the base field.
  • Degree — [E:F]=dim⁡FE[E : F] = \dim_F E[E:F]=dimF​E, the dimension of EEE as a vector space over FFF. The extension is finite if the degree is finite.
  • Generated extension — for α∈E\alpha \in Eα∈E, F(α)F(\alpha)F(α) is the smallest subfield of EEE containing FFF and α\alphaα. Likewise F(α1,…,αn)F(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n)F(α1​,…,αn​). An extension F(α)/FF(\alpha)/FF(α)/F is simple and α\alphaα is a primitive element.
  • Intermediate field — a field KKK with F⊆K⊆EF \subseteq K \subseteq EF⊆K⊆E.

Examples: [C:R]=2[\mathbb{C} : \mathbb{R}] = 2[C:R]=2 with basis 1,i1, i1,i. [Q(2):Q]=2[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2) : \mathbb{Q}] = 2[Q(2​):Q]=2 with basis 1,21, \sqrt21,2​, since Q(2)={a+b2:a,b∈Q}\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2) = \{a + b\sqrt2 : a, b \in \mathbb{Q}\}Q(2​)={a+b2​:a,b∈Q} and 2∉Q\sqrt2 \notin \mathbb{Q}2​∈/Q. [R:Q][\mathbb{R} : \mathbb{Q}][R:Q] is infinite (a countable field cannot span the uncountable R\mathbb{R}R with finitely many vectors). A field with qqq elements that contains Fp\mathbb{F}_pFp​ has q=pnq = p^nq=pn where n=[E:Fp]n = [E : \mathbb{F}_p]n=[E:Fp​], because an nnn-dimensional vector space over Fp\mathbb{F}_pFp​ has pnp^npn elements.

The tower law

Theorem (tower law). If F⊆K⊆EF \subseteq K \subseteq EF⊆K⊆E are fields, then

[E:F]=[E:K] [K:F],[E : F] = [E : K]\,[K : F], [E:F]=[E:K][K:F],

in the sense that the left side is finite exactly when both factors are, and then equality holds.

Proof (finite case). Let α1,…,αm\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_mα1​,…,αm​ be a basis of KKK over FFF and β1,…,βn\beta_1, \dots, \beta_nβ1​,…,βn​ a basis of EEE over KKK. The claim is that the mnmnmn products αiβj\alpha_i\beta_jαi​βj​ form a basis of EEE over FFF.

  • Spanning. Any e∈Ee \in Ee∈E is ∑jkjβj\sum_j k_j \beta_j∑j​kj​βj​ with kj∈Kk_j \in Kkj​∈K, and each kj=∑ifijαik_j = \sum_i f_{ij}\alpha_ikj​=∑i​fij​αi​ with fij∈Ff_{ij} \in Ffij​∈F. So e=∑i,jfij αiβje = \sum_{i,j} f_{ij}\,\alpha_i\beta_je=∑i,j​fij​αi​βj​.
  • Independence. If ∑i,jfijαiβj=0\sum_{i,j} f_{ij}\alpha_i\beta_j = 0∑i,j​fij​αi​βj​=0, regroup as ∑j(∑ifijαi)βj=0\sum_j \big(\sum_i f_{ij}\alpha_i\big)\beta_j = 0∑j​(∑i​fij​αi​)βj​=0. The inner sums are in KKK and the βj\beta_jβj​ are independent over KKK, so each inner sum is 000. The αi\alpha_iαi​ are independent over FFF, so every fij=0f_{ij} = 0fij​=0. ∎

Corollaries. (1) If KKK is intermediate in a finite extension E/FE/FE/F, then [K:F][K : F][K:F] divides [E:F][E : F][E:F]. (2) If [E:F][E : F][E:F] is prime, there is no intermediate field other than FFF and EEE. (3) If α∈E\alpha \in Eα∈E, then [F(α):F][F(\alpha) : F][F(α):F] divides [E:F][E : F][E:F].

Trick: most degree computations are "bound above by a tower, bound below by divisibility". If [K:F]=2[K : F] = 2[K:F]=2 and [L:F]=3[L : F] = 3[L:F]=3 are both inside EEE, then 6∣[E:F]6 \mid [E : F]6∣[E:F].

Chapter 2 — Algebraic elements and minimal polynomials

Terminology

  • Algebraic — α∈E\alpha \in Eα∈E is algebraic over FFF if f(α)=0f(\alpha) = 0f(α)=0 for some nonzero f∈F[x]f \in F[x]f∈F[x]. Otherwise α\alphaα is transcendental over FFF.
  • Algebraic extension — every element of EEE is algebraic over FFF.
  • Minimal polynomial — the monic polynomial mα∈F[x]m_\alpha \in F[x]mα​∈F[x] of least degree with mα(α)=0m_\alpha(\alpha) = 0mα​(α)=0.

2\sqrt22​, iii, 23\sqrt[3]{2}32​ and e2πi/5e^{2\pi i/5}e2πi/5 are algebraic over Q\mathbb{Q}Q. Hermite proved in 1873 that eee is transcendental and Lindemann in 1882 that π\piπ is transcendental; both proofs are analytic and are not needed below.

The minimal polynomial

Theorem. Let α\alphaα be algebraic over FFF. Then:

  1. mαm_\alphamα​ exists, is unique, and is irreducible over FFF;
  2. for f∈F[x]f \in F[x]f∈F[x]: f(α)=0f(\alpha) = 0f(α)=0 if and only if mα∣fm_\alpha \mid fmα​∣f;
  3. F(α)≅F[x]/(mα)F(\alpha) \cong F[x]/(m_\alpha)F(α)≅F[x]/(mα​), so [F(α):F]=deg⁡mα[F(\alpha) : F] = \deg m_\alpha[F(α):F]=degmα​, with basis 1,α,…,αn−11, \alpha, \dots, \alpha^{n-1}1,α,…,αn−1 where n=deg⁡mαn = \deg m_\alphan=degmα​.

Proof. Evaluation evα:F[x]→E\mathrm{ev}_\alpha : F[x] \to Eevα​:F[x]→E, f↦f(α)f \mapsto f(\alpha)f↦f(α), is a ring homomorphism. Its kernel III is nonzero because α\alphaα is algebraic, and F[x]F[x]F[x] is a PID (post 04), so I=(m)I = (m)I=(m) for a unique monic mmm; this mmm has least degree among nonzero elements of III, so m=mαm = m_\alpham=mα​, and statement 2 is "f∈I  ⟺  mα∣ff \in I \iff m_\alpha \mid ff∈I⟺mα​∣f". The image of evα\mathrm{ev}_\alphaevα​ is a subring of the field EEE, hence a domain, so by the First Isomorphism Theorem F[x]/(mα)F[x]/(m_\alpha)F[x]/(mα​) is a domain: (mα)(m_\alpha)(mα​) is prime, so mαm_\alphamα​ is irreducible. Then (mα)(m_\alpha)(mα​) is maximal (post 04, Chapter 6), so the image F[α]F[\alpha]F[α] is a field containing FFF and α\alphaα; it is therefore F(α)F(\alpha)F(α). The basis claim is the division algorithm: every class has a unique representative of degree <n< n<n. ∎

So to find [F(α):F][F(\alpha) : F][F(α):F]: find a polynomial with root α\alphaα and prove it irreducible with the tests of post 04.

Common pitfall: the minimal polynomial depends on the base field. m2m_{\sqrt2}m2​​ over Q\mathbb{Q}Q is x2−2x^2 - 2x2−2; over R\mathbb{R}R it is x−2x - \sqrt2x−2​.

Arithmetic in Q(23)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})Q(32​). Let a=23a = \sqrt[3]{2}a=32​, with ma=x3−2m_a = x^3 - 2ma​=x3−2 (Eisenstein at 2), so [Q(a):Q]=3[\mathbb{Q}(a) : \mathbb{Q}] = 3[Q(a):Q]=3 with basis 1,a,a21, a, a^21,a,a2. To invert 1+a1 + a1+a, use (1+a)(1−a+a2)=1+a3=3(1 + a)(1 - a + a^2) = 1 + a^3 = 3(1+a)(1−a+a2)=1+a3=3:

11+23=1−23+433.\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt[3]{2}} = \frac{1 - \sqrt[3]{2} + \sqrt[3]{4}}{3}. 1+32​1​=31−32​+34​​.

Consequently, if α\alphaα and β\betaβ are algebraic then F(α,β)F(\alpha, \beta)F(α,β) is finite (tower law), so α±β\alpha \pm \betaα±β, αβ\alpha\betaαβ and α/β\alpha/\betaα/β are algebraic too: the algebraic numbers form a field.

Worked example: Q(√2, √3)

Degree. [Q(2):Q]=2[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2) : \mathbb{Q}] = 2[Q(2​):Q]=2. with basis 1,2,3,61, \sqrt2, \sqrt3, \sqrt61,2​,3​,6​ (products of the two bases, as in the proof of the tower law).

θ4−10θ2+1=0.\theta^4 - 10\theta^2 + 1 = 0. θ4−10θ2+1=0.

Chapter 3 — Ruler and compass

Start with the points 000 and 111 in the plane C\mathbb{C}C. A ruler draws the line through two constructed points; a compass draws a circle with a constructed centre through a constructed point. New points are intersections of lines and circles. A real number is constructible if it is a coordinate of a constructible point.

Key observation. If all points so far have coordinates in a field KKK, then:

  • the intersection of two lines solves a linear system, so it has coordinates in KKK;
  • an intersection involving a circle solves a quadratic equation over KKK, so it has coordinates in KKK or in some K(d)K(\sqrt d)K(d​) with d∈Kd \in Kd∈K, an extension of degree 2.

Theorem. If α\alphaα is constructible, then [Q(α):Q][\mathbb{Q}(\alpha) : \mathbb{Q}][Q(α):Q] is a power of 2.

Proof. By the observation, α\alphaα lies in the top field of a tower Q=K0⊂K1⊂⋯⊂Kr\mathbb{Q} = K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots \subset K_rQ=K0​⊂K1​⊂⋯⊂Kr​ with each [Ki+1:Ki]=2[K_{i+1} : K_i] = 2[Ki+1​:Ki​]=2. By the tower law [Kr:Q]=2r[K_r : \mathbb{Q}] = 2^r[Kr​:Q]=2r, and [Q(α):Q][\mathbb{Q}(\alpha) : \mathbb{Q}][Q(α):Q] divides it. ∎

Doubling the cube. A cube of volume 2 needs side 23\sqrt[3]{2}32​, whose minimal polynomial x3−2x^3 - 2x3−2 has degree 3. Not a power of 2, so impossible.

Trisecting 60°. A 60° angle is constructible (equilateral triangle). Trisecting it means constructing c=cos⁡20∘c = \cos 20^\circc=cos20∘. From cos⁡3θ=4cos⁡3θ−3cos⁡θ\cos 3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\thetacos3θ=4cos3θ−3cosθ with θ=20∘\theta = 20^\circθ=20∘ and cos⁡60∘=12\cos 60^\circ = \tfrac12cos60∘=21​:

4c3−3c=12⟺8c3−6c−1=0.4c^3 - 3c = \tfrac12 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 8c^3 - 6c - 1 = 0. 4c3−3c=21​⟺8c3−6c−1=0.

By the rational root test, a rational root would be one of ±1,±12,±14,±18\pm1, \pm\tfrac12, \pm\tfrac14, \pm\tfrac18±1,±21​,±41​,±81​; substituting gives 1,−3,−3,1,−198,38,−11164,−17641, -3, -3, 1, -\tfrac{19}{8}, \tfrac38, -\tfrac{111}{64}, -\tfrac{17}{64}1,−3,−3,1,−819​,83​,−64111​,−6417​, never 000. A cubic without rational roots is irreducible, so [Q(c):Q]=3[\mathbb{Q}(c) : \mathbb{Q}] = 3[Q(c):Q]=3 and the trisection is impossible. (Some angles, such as 90°, can be trisected; the theorem is that no method works for every angle.)

Squaring the circle. A square of area π\piπ needs side π\sqrt\piπ​. If π\sqrt\piπ​ were constructible it would be algebraic, so π\piπ would be algebraic, contradicting Lindemann.

Watch out: "degree a power of 2" is necessary, not sufficient. The exact criterion is that the splitting field of the minimal polynomial has degree a power of 2. The Gauss–Wantzel theorem answers the polygon question: a regular nnn-gon is constructible if and only if nnn is a power of 2 times a product of distinct Fermat primes 3,5,17,257,655373, 5, 17, 257, 655373,5,17,257,65537.

Chapter 4 — Splitting fields and finite fields

Splitting fields

A splitting field of a nonconstant f∈F[x]f \in F[x]f∈F[x] is an extension E/FE/FE/F in which fff factors into linear factors, f=c(x−α1)⋯(x−αn)f = c(x - \alpha_1)\cdots(x - \alpha_n)f=c(x−α1​)⋯(x−αn​), and which is generated by the roots: E=F(α1,…,αn)E = F(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n)E=F(α1​,…,αn​).

Theorem. Every nonconstant f∈F[x]f \in F[x]f∈F[x] has a splitting field EEE, with [E:F]≤n![E : F] \le n![E:F]≤n! where n=deg⁡fn = \deg fn=degf. Any two splitting fields of fff over FFF are isomorphic by an isomorphism that fixes FFF.

(Existence: take an irreducible factor ppp of fff; in F[x]/(p)F[x]/(p)F[x]/(p) it has a root (post 04), so fff gains a linear factor over an extension of degree ≤n\le n≤n; repeat on the quotient, whose degree is n−1n - 1n−1. Uniqueness is proved by the same induction, extending an isomorphism one root at a time.)

Examples:

  • x2−2x^2 - 2x2−2 over Q\mathbb{Q}Q: splitting field Q(2)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)Q(2​), degree 2.
  • x4−10x2+1x^4 - 10x^2 + 1x4−10x2+1: roots ±2±3\pm\sqrt2 \pm \sqrt3±2​±3​, splitting field Q(2,3)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2, \sqrt3)Q(2​,3​), degree 4.
  • x3−2x^3 - 2x3−2: roots α\alphaα, αω\alpha\omegaαω, αω2\alpha\omega^2αω2 with α=23\alpha = \sqrt[3]{2}α=32​ and ω=e2πi/3\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}ω=e2πi/3, a root of x2+x+1x^2 + x + 1x2+x+1. The splitting field is E=Q(α,ω)E = \mathbb{Q}(\alpha, \omega)E=Q(α,ω) (it contains ω=αω/α\omega = \alpha\omega/\alphaω=αω/α). [Q(α):Q]=3[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha) : \mathbb{Q}] = 3[Q(α):Q]=3, and ω∉Q(α)⊂R\omega \notin \mathbb{Q}(\alpha) \subset \mathbb{R}ω∈/Q(α)⊂R, so [E:Q(α)]=2[E : \mathbb{Q}(\alpha)] = 2[E:Q(α)]=2. Hence [E:Q]=6=3![E : \mathbb{Q}] = 6 = 3![E:Q]=6=3!, the maximum.

Finite fields

Let EEE be a finite field. Its characteristic is a prime ppp (post 04), so it contains Fp\mathbb{F}_pFp​ and has pnp^npn elements, n=[E:Fp]n = [E : \mathbb{F}_p]n=[E:Fp​].

Lemma (freshman's dream). In a commutative ring of characteristic ppp, (a+b)p=ap+bp(a + b)^p = a^p + b^p(a+b)p=ap+bp.

Proof. Expand with the binomial theorem. For 0<k<p0 < k < p0<k<p, (pk)=p!k!(p−k)!\binom{p}{k} = \frac{p!}{k!(p-k)!}(kp​)=k!(p−k)!p!​ is divisible by ppp: ppp divides the numerator but not the denominator. So all middle terms vanish. ∎

Hence the Frobenius map Fr(a)=ap\mathrm{Fr}(a) = a^pFr(a)=ap is a ring homomorphism. On a field it is injective (post 04: homomorphisms out of fields are injective), so on a finite field it is an automorphism, and it fixes exactly the elements of Fp\mathbb{F}_pFp​ (the roots of xp−xx^p - xxp−x; there are at most ppp of them, and all of Fp\mathbb{F}_pFp​ qualifies by Fermat's little theorem from post 00).

Theorem (existence and uniqueness of finite fields). For every prime ppp and n≥1n \ge 1n≥1 there is a field with q=pnq = p^nq=pn elements, and any two such fields are isomorphic. It is written Fq\mathbb{F}_qFq​.

Proof. Existence. Let EEE be a splitting field of g=xq−xg = x^q - xg=xq−x over Fp\mathbb{F}_pFp​, and SSS the set of roots of ggg in EEE. The derivative g′=qxq−1−1=−1g' = qx^{q-1} - 1 = -1g′=qxq−1−1=−1 has no common root with ggg, so the roots are distinct and ∣S∣=q|S| = q∣S∣=q. SSS is a subfield: if aq=aa^q = aaq=a and bq=bb^q = bbq=b, then (a+b)q=aq+bq=a+b(a + b)^q = a^q + b^q = a + b(a+b)q=aq+bq=a+b (apply the lemma nnn times), (ab)q=ab(ab)^q = ab(ab)q=ab, and (a−1)q=a−1(a^{-1})^q = a^{-1}(a−1)q=a−1. A subfield containing all roots is the whole splitting field, so E=SE = SE=S has qqq elements.

Uniqueness. In any field KKK with qqq elements, the multiplicative group has order q−1q - 1q−1, so aq−1=1a^{q-1} = 1aq−1=1 for a≠0a \ne 0a=0 by Lagrange, and aq=aa^q = aaq=a for all aaa. So KKK consists of the qqq roots of xq−xx^q - xxq−x, and is a splitting field of xq−xx^q - xxq−x over Fp\mathbb{F}_pFp​. Splitting fields are unique up to isomorphism. ∎

Two further facts, stated without proof: the multiplicative group Fq×\mathbb{F}_q^\timesFq×​ is cyclic (post 04's F8\mathbb{F}_8F8​ table showed a generator), and Fpd\mathbb{F}_{p^d}Fpd​ sits inside Fpn\mathbb{F}_{p^n}Fpn​ exactly when d∣nd \mid nd∣n.

Worked example. Over F2\mathbb{F}_2F2​:

x4−x=x (x+1) (x2+x+1),x8−x=x (x+1) (x3+x+1) (x3+x2+1).\begin{aligned} x^4 - x &= x\,(x + 1)\,(x^2 + x + 1), \\ x^8 - x &= x\,(x + 1)\,(x^3 + x + 1)\,(x^3 + x^2 + 1). \end{aligned} x4−xx8−x​=x(x+1)(x2+x+1),=x(x+1)(x3+x+1)(x3+x2+1).​

The first line lists the minimal polynomials of the 4 elements of F4\mathbb{F}_4F4​; the second those of the 8 elements of F8\mathbb{F}_8F8​. The two cubics are the two irreducible cubics over F2\mathbb{F}_2F2​, each with three roots in F8\mathbb{F}_8F8​. No quadratic appears in the second line, matching 2∤32 \nmid 32∤3: F4⊈F8\mathbb{F}_4 \not\subseteq \mathbb{F}_8F4​⊆F8​.

Chapter 5 — Galois extensions and the Galois group

Terminology

  • FFF-automorphism of EEE — a field automorphism σ:E→E\sigma : E \to Eσ:E→E with σ(a)=a\sigma(a) = aσ(a)=a for every a∈Fa \in Fa∈F. They form a group Aut⁡(E/F)\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)Aut(E/F).
  • Fixed field — for a subgroup H≤Aut⁡(E)H \le \operatorname{Aut}(E)H≤Aut(E), EH={e∈E:σ(e)=e for all σ∈H}E^H = \{ e \in E : \sigma(e) = e \text{ for all } \sigma \in H \}EH={e∈E:σ(e)=e for all σ∈H}.
  • Separable polynomial — one with no repeated root in its splitting field. An algebraic extension is separable if every minimal polynomial is separable.
  • Normal extension — an algebraic E/FE/FE/F such that every irreducible polynomial in F[x]F[x]F[x] with one root in EEE splits completely in EEE.
  • Galois extension — a finite extension that is normal and separable. Its Galois group is Gal⁡(E/F)=Aut⁡(E/F)\operatorname{Gal}(E/F) = \operatorname{Aut}(E/F)Gal(E/F)=Aut(E/F).
  • Galois group of a polynomial — Gal⁡(E/F)\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)Gal(E/F) for EEE a splitting field of the (separable) polynomial.

Separability is automatic in the cases you meet most. Over a field of characteristic 0, and over any finite field, every irreducible polynomial is separable. (An irreducible fff has a repeated root only if gcd⁡(f,f′)≠1\gcd(f, f') \ne 1gcd(f,f′)=1, which forces f′=0f' = 0f′=0; in characteristic 0 that is impossible for nonconstant fff.) The standard inseparable example is xp−tx^p - txp−t over the field Fp(t)\mathbb{F}_p(t)Fp​(t) of rational functions: it is irreducible (Eisenstein at the prime ttt), but over its splitting field it equals (x−t1/p)p(x - t^{1/p})^p(x−t1/p)p.

Automorphisms permute roots

Lemma. If f∈F[x]f \in F[x]f∈F[x], α∈E\alpha \in Eα∈E is a root of fff, and σ∈Aut⁡(E/F)\sigma \in \operatorname{Aut}(E/F)σ∈Aut(E/F), then σ(α)\sigma(\alpha)σ(α) is a root of fff.

Proof. If f=∑ckxkf = \sum c_k x^kf=∑ck​xk with ck∈Fc_k \in Fck​∈F, then f(σ(α))=∑ckσ(α)k=σ(∑ckαk)=σ(0)=0f(\sigma(\alpha)) = \sum c_k \sigma(\alpha)^k = \sigma\big(\sum c_k\alpha^k\big) = \sigma(0) = 0f(σ(α))=∑ck​σ(α)k=σ(∑ck​αk)=σ(0)=0, since σ\sigmaσ fixes each ckc_kck​. ∎

So if E=F(α1,…,αn)E = F(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n)E=F(α1​,…,αn​) is a splitting field of fff, an FFF-automorphism is determined by how it permutes α1,…,αn\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_nα1​,…,αn​, and Aut⁡(E/F)\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)Aut(E/F) is (isomorphic to) a subgroup of SnS_nSn​, an action on the roots in the sense of post 03.

Theorem (characterisations of Galois extensions). For a finite extension E/FE/FE/F the following are equivalent:

  1. E/FE/FE/F is Galois (normal and separable);
  2. EEE is the splitting field over FFF of a separable polynomial;
  3. ∣Aut⁡(E/F)∣=[E:F]\lvert\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)\rvert = [E : F]∣Aut(E/F)∣=[E:F];
  4. the fixed field of Aut⁡(E/F)\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)Aut(E/F) is exactly FFF.

In general ∣Aut⁡(E/F)∣≤[E:F]\lvert\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)\rvert \le [E : F]∣Aut(E/F)∣≤[E:F] and equality is what "Galois" means in practice.

Examples.

  • Gal⁡(C/R)={id,complex conjugation}≅Z/2Z\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{R}) = \{\mathrm{id}, \text{complex conjugation}\} \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}Gal(C/R)={id,complex conjugation}≅Z/2Z.
  • Q(23)/Q\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})/\mathbb{Q}Q(32​)/Q is not Galois. An automorphism must send 23\sqrt[3]{2}32​ to a root of x3−2x^3 - 2x3−2 inside Q(23)⊂R\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2}) \subset \mathbb{R}Q(32​)⊂R, and the only real root is 23\sqrt[3]{2}32​ itself. So Aut⁡\operatorname{Aut}Aut is trivial, of order 1<31 < 31<3. It fails normality: x3−2x^3 - 2x3−2 has one root in the field but does not split there.
  • Gal⁡(Fpn/Fp)\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{p^n}/\mathbb{F}_p)Gal(Fpn​/Fp​) is cyclic of order nnn, generated by Frobenius. (Frk\mathrm{Fr}^kFrk fixes exactly the roots of xpk−xx^{p^k} - xxpk−x, so Fr\mathrm{Fr}Fr has order exactly nnn; and the group has order [Fpn:Fp]=n[\mathbb{F}_{p^n} : \mathbb{F}_p] = n[Fpn​:Fp​]=n because Fpn\mathbb{F}_{p^n}Fpn​ is the splitting field of the separable xpn−xx^{p^n} - xxpn−x.)

Chapter 6 — The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory

Theorem (Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory). Let E/FE/FE/F be a finite Galois extension with group G=Gal⁡(E/F)G = \operatorname{Gal}(E/F)G=Gal(E/F). Then the maps

H⟼EHandK⟼Gal⁡(E/K)H \longmapsto E^H \qquad\text{and}\qquad K \longmapsto \operatorname{Gal}(E/K) H⟼EHandK⟼Gal(E/K)

are mutually inverse bijections between subgroups H≤GH \le GH≤G and intermediate fields F⊆K⊆EF \subseteq K \subseteq EF⊆K⊆E, and:

  1. they reverse inclusion: H1≤H2H_1 \le H_2H1​≤H2​ if and only if EH1⊇EH2E^{H_1} \supseteq E^{H_2}EH1​⊇EH2​;
  2. degrees match indices: [E:EH]=∣H∣[E : E^H] = |H|[E:EH]=∣H∣ and [EH:F]=[G:H][E^H : F] = [G : H][EH:F]=[G:H];
  3. K/FK/FK/F is Galois if and only if Gal⁡(E/K)\operatorname{Gal}(E/K)Gal(E/K) is a normal subgroup of GGG, and then Gal⁡(K/F)≅G/Gal⁡(E/K)\operatorname{Gal}(K/F) \cong G / \operatorname{Gal}(E/K)Gal(K/F)≅G/Gal(E/K).

So the lattice of intermediate fields is the lattice of subgroups turned upside down: the big field EEE matches the trivial group, the base FFF matches all of GGG. Part 3 is where normal subgroups and quotient groups (post 02) acquire their original meaning.

E=Q(2,3)E = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2, \sqrt3)E=Q(2​,3​) is the splitting field of the separable (x2−2)(x2−3)(x^2 - 2)(x^2 - 3)(x2−2)(x2−3), so it is Galois of degree 4 and GGG has 4 elements. Common pitfall: the correspondence reverses order. A bigger subgroup fixes more conditions and so has a smaller fixed field. Draw the two lattices with EEE at the top and {id}\{\mathrm{id}\}{id} at the top.

Chapter 7 — Solvable groups and the quintic

Solvable groups

A group GGG is solvable if there is a chain of subgroups

{e}=G0⊴G1⊴⋯⊴Gk=G\{e\} = G_0 \trianglelefteq G_1 \trianglelefteq \cdots \trianglelefteq G_k = G {e}=G0​⊴G1​⊴⋯⊴Gk​=G

with each GiG_iGi​ normal in Gi+1G_{i+1}Gi+1​ and each quotient Gi+1/GiG_{i+1}/G_iGi+1​/Gi​ abelian.

  • Abelian groups are solvable (k=1k = 1k=1).
  • S3S_3S3​: {e}⊴A3⊴S3\{e\} \trianglelefteq A_3 \trianglelefteq S_3{e}⊴A3​⊴S3​ with quotients Z/3\mathbb{Z}/3Z/3 and Z/2\mathbb{Z}/2Z/2.
  • S4S_4S4​: {e}⊴V4⊴A4⊴S4\{e\} \trianglelefteq V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4 \trianglelefteq S_4{e}⊴V4​⊴A4​⊴S4​ with quotients Z/2×Z/2\mathbb{Z}/2 \times \mathbb{Z}/2Z/2×Z/2, Z/3\mathbb{Z}/3Z/3, Z/2\mathbb{Z}/2Z/2. So every subgroup of S4S_4S4​ is solvable too (subgroups and quotients of solvable groups are solvable).
  • S5S_5S5​ is not solvable. Its only normal subgroups are {e}\{e\}{e}, A5A_5A5​, S5S_5S5​, and A5A_5A5​ is simple and non-abelian (post 02). A chain would have to pass through A5A_5A5​, and the step below A5A_5A5​ would need a normal subgroup of A5A_5A5​ with abelian quotient; the only candidates are A5A_5A5​ itself (quotient trivial, no progress) and {e}\{e\}{e} (quotient A5A_5A5​, not abelian). Equivalently, the commutator subgroup of A5A_5A5​ is A5A_5A5​, so the derived series S5⊃A5⊃A5⊃⋯S_5 \supset A_5 \supset A_5 \supset \cdotsS5​⊃A5​⊃A5​⊃⋯ never reaches {e}\{e\}{e}.

Radicals

A polynomial f∈Q[x]f \in \mathbb{Q}[x]f∈Q[x] is solvable by radicals if its roots can be written starting from rational numbers using +,−,×,÷+, -, \times, \div+,−,×,÷ and kkk-th roots. The quadratic formula shows this for degree 2; Cardano's and Ferrari's formulas do it for degrees 3 and 4.

Theorem (Galois, characteristic 0). fff is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is solvable.

(Idea of "only if": adjoining a kkk-th root to a field that already contains the kkk-th roots of unity gives a Galois extension with cyclic group; adjoining roots of unity gives an abelian group. A tower of such steps gives, through part 3 of the Fundamental Theorem, a chain of normal subgroups with abelian quotients.)

Since S4S_4S4​ is solvable and the Galois group of a degree-nnn polynomial embeds in SnS_nSn​, every polynomial of degree ≤4\le 4≤4 is solvable by radicals. The Abel–Ruffini theorem says the general quintic is not: the generic polynomial x5+a4x4+⋯+a0x^5 + a_4x^4 + \cdots + a_0x5+a4​x4+⋯+a0​ with independent indeterminate coefficients has Galois group S5S_5S5​ over Q(a0,…,a4)\mathbb{Q}(a_0, \dots, a_4)Q(a0​,…,a4​), which is not solvable, so there is no formula in radicals valid for all quintics. Galois theory gives more: specific quintics with rational coefficients have unsolvable roots.

A concrete unsolvable quintic

Lemma. Let ppp be prime and f∈Q[x]f \in \mathbb{Q}[x]f∈Q[x] irreducible of degree ppp with exactly two non-real roots. Then Gal⁡(f)≅Sp\operatorname{Gal}(f) \cong S_pGal(f)≅Sp​.

Proof. View G=Gal⁡(f)G = \operatorname{Gal}(f)G=Gal(f) as a subgroup of SpS_pSp​ acting on the ppp roots. For a root α\alphaα, [Q(α):Q]=p[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha) : \mathbb{Q}] = p[Q(α):Q]=p divides [E:Q]=∣G∣[E : \mathbb{Q}] = |G|[E:Q]=∣G∣, so by Cauchy's theorem (post 03) GGG has an element of order ppp; in SpS_pSp​ the elements of order ppp are the ppp-cycles. Complex conjugation restricts to an element of GGG that swaps the two non-real roots and fixes the p−2p - 2p−2 real ones: a transposition. For prime ppp, a ppp-cycle and a transposition generate all of SpS_pSp​. ∎

Theorem. f(x)=x5−4x+2f(x) = x^5 - 4x + 2f(x)=x5−4x+2 is not solvable by radicals over Q\mathbb{Q}Q.

Proof. Irreducible: Eisenstein at p=2p = 2p=2 (2∣−42 \mid -42∣−4, 2∣22 \mid 22∣2, 4∤24 \nmid 24∤2, leading coefficient 1).

Exactly three real roots: f′(x)=5x4−4f'(x) = 5x^4 - 4f′(x)=5x4−4 vanishes only at x=±cx = \pm cx=±c with c=(4/5)1/4≈0.9457c = (4/5)^{1/4} \approx 0.9457c=(4/5)1/4≈0.9457. So fff increases, then decreases on [−c,c][-c, c][−c,c], then increases. The local maximum f(−c)≈5.03>0f(-c) \approx 5.03 > 0f(−c)≈5.03>0 and the local minimum f(c)≈−1.03<0f(c) \approx -1.03 < 0f(c)≈−1.03<0, while f→−∞f \to -\inftyf→−∞ as x→−∞x \to -\inftyx→−∞ and f→+∞f \to +\inftyf→+∞ as x→+∞x \to +\inftyx→+∞. So fff crosses zero once on each of the three monotone pieces: three real roots, approximately −1.5185-1.5185−1.5185, 0.50850.50850.5085 and 1.24361.24361.2436, and the other two roots are a complex-conjugate pair.

By the lemma with p=5p = 5p=5, Gal⁡(f)≅S5\operatorname{Gal}(f) \cong S_5Gal(f)≅S5​, which is not solvable. By Galois's theorem, fff is not solvable by radicals. ∎

Watch out: "not solvable by radicals" does not mean the roots are hard to compute. Numerically they are easy (the values above). It means there is no finite expression in +,−,×,÷, k+, -, \times, \div, \sqrt[k]{\ }+,−,×,÷,k ​ for them.

Practice Exercises

1. Find [Q(2,23):Q][\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2, \sqrt[3]{2}) : \mathbb{Q}][Q(2​,32​):Q].

Solution

Q(2)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)Q(2​) has degree 2 and Q(23)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})Q(32​) has degree 3, both intermediate, so 2 and 3 divide the degree, and so does 6. On the other hand [Q(2,23):Q(23)]≤2[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2, \sqrt[3]{2}) : \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})] \le 2[Q(2​,32​):Q(32​)]≤2 (root of x2−2x^2 - 2x2−2), so the degree is at most 2⋅3=62 \cdot 3 = 62⋅3=6. Hence it is exactly 6.

2. Find the minimal polynomial of 2+i\sqrt2 + i2​+i over Q\mathbb{Q}Q.

Solution

Let θ=2+i\theta = \sqrt2 + iθ=2​+i. Then θ2=1+22 i\theta^2 = 1 + 2\sqrt2\,iθ2=1+22​i, so (θ2−1)2=−8(\theta^2 - 1)^2 = -8(θ2−1)2=−8, giving θ4−2θ2+9=0\theta^4 - 2\theta^2 + 9 = 0θ4−2θ2+9=0. As in the 2+3\sqrt2 + \sqrt32​+3​ example, Q(θ)=Q(2,i)\mathbb{Q}(\theta) = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2, i)Q(θ)=Q(2​,i), which has degree 4 (i∉Q(2)⊂Ri \notin \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2) \subset \mathbb{R}i∈/Q(2​)⊂R). So mθ=x4−2x2+9m_\theta = x^4 - 2x^2 + 9mθ​=x4−2x2+9.

3. Show that the regular 7-gon is not constructible, using that 2cos⁡(2π/7)2\cos(2\pi/7)2cos(2π/7) is a root of x3+x2−2x−1x^3 + x^2 - 2x - 1x3+x2−2x−1.

Solution

Rational roots could only be ±1\pm 1±1, which give −1-1−1 and 111, so the cubic has no rational root and is irreducible. Then [Q(2cos⁡(2π/7)):Q]=3[\mathbb{Q}(2\cos(2\pi/7)) : \mathbb{Q}] = 3[Q(2cos(2π/7)):Q]=3, not a power of 2, so cos⁡(2π/7)\cos(2\pi/7)cos(2π/7) is not constructible, and neither is the 7-gon. (Consistent with Gauss–Wantzel: 7 is prime but not a Fermat prime.)

4. List all subfields of F64\mathbb{F}_{64}F64​ and draw their inclusions. What is Gal⁡(F64/F2)\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{64}/\mathbb{F}_2)Gal(F64​/F2​)?

Solution

64=2664 = 2^664=26 and the divisors of 6 are 1, 2, 3, 6, so the subfields are F2,F4,F8,F64\mathbb{F}_2, \mathbb{F}_4, \mathbb{F}_8, \mathbb{F}_{64}F2​,F4​,F8​,F64​. Inclusions: F2⊂F4⊂F64\mathbb{F}_2 \subset \mathbb{F}_4 \subset \mathbb{F}_{64}F2​⊂F4​⊂F64​ and F2⊂F8⊂F64\mathbb{F}_2 \subset \mathbb{F}_8 \subset \mathbb{F}_{64}F2​⊂F8​⊂F64​, while F4⊈F8\mathbb{F}_4 \not\subseteq \mathbb{F}_8F4​⊆F8​. The Galois group is cyclic of order 6, generated by Frobenius; its subgroups (orders 1, 2, 3, 6) match the subfields F64,F8,F4,F2\mathbb{F}_{64}, \mathbb{F}_8, \mathbb{F}_4, \mathbb{F}_2F64​,F8​,F4​,F2​ in that order.

5. In Q(2,3)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2, \sqrt3)Q(2​,3​), which automorphism fixes 6\sqrt66​, and what is the fixed field of {id,σ}\{\mathrm{id}, \sigma\}{id,σ}? Why does the Fundamental Theorem guarantee that Q(2+3)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2 + \sqrt3)Q(2​+3​) is the whole field without computing θ3\theta^3θ3?

Solution

στ\sigma\tauστ fixes 6\sqrt66​ (both signs flip). σ\sigmaσ fixes 3\sqrt33​, so E⟨σ⟩⊇Q(3)E^{\langle\sigma\rangle} \supseteq \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt3)E⟨σ⟩⊇Q(3​), and both have degree 2, so they are equal. For θ=2+3\theta = \sqrt2 + \sqrt3θ=2​+3​: the non-identity automorphisms send θ\thetaθ to −2+3-\sqrt2 + \sqrt3−2​+3​, 2−3\sqrt2 - \sqrt32​−3​, −2−3-\sqrt2 - \sqrt3−2​−3​, all different from θ\thetaθ. So only the trivial subgroup fixes θ\thetaθ, and Q(θ)\mathbb{Q}(\theta)Q(θ) corresponds to {id}\{\mathrm{id}\}{id}, i.e. it is all of EEE.

6. Explain why every polynomial of degree at most 4 over Q\mathbb{Q}Q is solvable by radicals, but this argument says nothing about degree 5.

Solution

The Galois group of a degree-nnn polynomial is a subgroup of SnS_nSn​. For n≤4n \le 4n≤4, SnS_nSn​ is solvable (chains above), and subgroups of solvable groups are solvable, so Galois's theorem applies. For n=5n = 5n=5 the group may be a solvable subgroup of S5S_5S5​ (for example x5−2x^5 - 2x5−2 is solvable by radicals, since 25\sqrt[5]{2}52​ is already a radical), or all of S5S_5S5​, as for x5−4x+2x^5 - 4x + 2x5−4x+2. The degree alone does not decide.

Frobenius a↦apa \mapsto a^pa↦ap; generates Gal⁡(Fpn/Fp)≅Z/n\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{p^n}/\mathbb{F}_p) \cong \mathbb{Z}/nGal(Fpn​/Fp​)≅Z/n
Galois extension normal and separable; ∣Aut⁡(E/F)∣=[E:F]\lvert\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)\rvert = [E : F]∣Aut(E/F)∣=[E:F]
Fundamental Theorem subgroups ↔ intermediate fields, order-reversing; normal ↔ Galois
x3−2x^3 - 2x3−2 splitting field degree 6, group S3S_3S3​, subfield Q(ω)\mathbb{Q}(\omega)Q(ω) ↔ A3A_3A3​
Solvable group chain of normal steps with abelian quotients; S4S_4S4​ yes, S5S_5S5​ no
Galois's criterion solvable by radicals ⇔ solvable Galois group (char 0)
Unsolvable quintic x5−4x+2x^5 - 4x + 2x5−4x+2: Eisenstein at 2, three real roots, group S5S_5S5​

What's next

This post completes the core course: from the integers and modular arithmetic (post 00), through groups, actions and Sylow theory (posts 01–03), rings and fields (post 04), to Galois theory. The table below lists the planned extensions. Each builds directly on the material here, so the series can grow without renumbering the existing posts.

Planned future extensions

Post Topic What it covers
06 Modules and linear algebra over rings Modules, free modules, the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID; the finite abelian groups of post 03 and the rational and Jordan canonical forms as two special cases
07 Representation theory of finite groups Group representations, Maschke's theorem, Schur's lemma, characters and orthogonality, character tables of S3S_3S3​, S4S_4S4​ and A5A_5A5​
08 Algebraic number theory Rings of integers, Dedekind domains, how unique factorisation of ideals repairs Z[−5]\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]Z[−5​], the class group, cyclotomic fields
09 Commutative algebra and a first look at algebraic geometry Noetherian rings, the Hilbert basis theorem, localisation, the Nullstellensatz, varieties and their coordinate rings
10 Algebra in cryptography Finite-field arithmetic in practice (AES uses F28\mathbb{F}_{2^8}F28​), Diffie–Hellman and discrete logarithms, elliptic-curve groups, lattices and lattice-based cryptography

References

  • D. S. Dummit and R. M. Foote, Abstract Algebra, 3rd edition, Wiley, 2004 — Chapters 13 (field extensions, constructions, splitting fields, finite fields) and 14 (Galois theory, finite fields, Galois groups of polynomials, solvability by radicals).
  • M. Artin, Algebra, 2nd edition, Pearson, 2011 — Chapters 15 (fields, ruler and compass) and 16 (Galois theory, quintic equations).
  • I. Stewart, Galois Theory, 4th edition, CRC Press, 2015 — a readable, historically informed development, including Abel–Ruffini.
  • J. S. Milne, Fields and Galois Theory, course notes (free).
  • E. Artin, Galois Theory, Notre Dame Mathematical Lectures 2, 1942 (Dover reprint) — the classic linear-algebra approach to the Fundamental Theorem.
  • MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.702 Algebra II (Spring 2011) — lecture notes on fields and Galois theory.
  • K. Conrad, Expository papers ("blurbs") — short notes on Galois theory, including Galois groups of cubics and quartics.

Note: this post is in progress. Planned additions: a full proof of the Fundamental Theorem (Artin's lemma on fixed fields), cyclotomic extensions and the constructible 17-gon, the discriminant as a test for Gal⁡⊆An\operatorname{Gal} \subseteq A_nGal⊆An​, and a worked Cardano solution of a cubic read through its Galois group.
